source_text: Vae, ait, per quem traditur filius hominis. ergo iam 'uae* constat imprecationis et comminationis inclamationem intellegendam et irato et offenso deputandam, nisi si ludas impune erat tantum sceleris relaturus. at si impune, uacat 'uae'; si non impune, utique ab eo puniendus, in quem scelus traditionis admisit. porro si sciens passus est hominem, quem ipse comitatui suo adsciuerat, in tantum scelus ruere, noli iam de creatore circa Adam retractare quae in tuum quoque deum retorquentur: aut ignorasse illum, qui non ex prouidentia obstitit peccaturo, aut obsistere non potuisse, si (non) ignorabat, aut noluisse, si et sciebat et poterat, atque ita malitiosum iudicandum, qui passus sit hominem suum ex delicto perire. suadeo igitur agnoscas potius et in isto creatorem quam parem illi deum optimum aduersus sententiam tuam facias. nam et Petrum praesumptorie aliquid elocutum negationi potius destinando zeloten deum tibi ostendit. debuit etiam osculo tradi, propheticus scilicet Christus, ut eius scilicet filius, qui labiis a populo diligebatur. Perductus in consessum, an ipse esset Christus, interrogatur. de quo Christo Iudaei quaesissent nisi de suo? cur ergo non uel tunc alium eis prodidit? 'ut pati posset', inquis, id est, ut ille optimus ignorantes adhuc in scelus mergeret. atquin et si dixisset, passurus esset. si dixero enim, inquit, uobis, non credetis. porro non credituri perseuerassent in necem eius. et cur non magis passurus esset, si alterius dei ac per hoc aduersarium creatoris (se) manifestasset? ergo non, ut pateretur, alium se tunc quoque supersedit ostendere, sed quoniam ex ore eius confessionem extorquere cupiebant, nec confesso tamen credituri, qui eum ex operibus scripturas adimplentibus agnouisse debuerant. ita eius fuit occultasse se, cui ultro debebatur agnitio. et tamen adhuc eis manum porrigens: abhinc, inquit, erit filius hominis sedens ad dexteram uirtutis dei. suggerebat enim se esse (de) Danihelis prophetia (filium hominis* et de psalmo Dauid (sedentem ad dexteram dei'. itaque ex isto dicto et scripturae comparatione inluminati, quem se uellet intellegi: ergo, inquiunt, tu dei filius es? cuius dei, nisi quem solum nouerant? cuius dei, nisi quem in psalmo meminerant dixisse filio suo: sede ad dexteram meam? <sed respondit: uos dicitis, quasi: non ego atquin confirmauit id se esse, quod illi dixerant, dum rursus interrogant. unde autem probabis interrogatiuo et non (et) ipsos confirmatiuo pronuntiasse: ergo tu filius dei es, ut, quia oblique ostenderat se per scripturas filium dei intellegendum, sic senserint: 'ergo tu dei es filius', quod te non uis aperte dicere? atque ita et ille (uos dicitis' confirmatiue respondit, et adeo sic fuit pronuntiatio eius, ut perseuerauerint in eo, quod pronuntiatio sapiebat.
pass_a_gloss: Woe, he says, through whom the Son of Man is betrayed. Therefore, now 'woe' is understood to be an exclamation of imprecation and commination, and to be attributed to one who is angry and offended, unless he who was going to relate such a great crime was playing innocently. But if innocently, 'woe' is empty; if not innocently, certainly he is to be punished, in whom the crime of betrayal was committed. Furthermore, if he knowingly allowed the man, whom he himself had added to his company, to rush into such a great crime, do not now retract about the Creator concerning Adam what can also be turned against your own god: either he was ignorant, because he did not prevent the one who was about to sin, or he was unable to prevent, if he was not ignorant, or he did not want to, if he both knew and was able, and thus is to be judged malicious, who allowed his man to perish through fault. I advise, therefore, that you rather recognize the Creator in this one and make him equal to that best god against your opinion. For also Peter, having spoken something presumptuously, shows a zealous god to you by destining it to negation. He ought to have been betrayed even with a kiss, namely the prophetic Christ, so that he, the Son, who was loved by the people with their lips. Having been led into the council, he is asked if he himself is the Christ. About which Christ the Jews would have asked, unless about their own? Why, therefore, did he not betray another to them even then? 'So that he might suffer,' you say, that is, so that he might plunge the ignorant still into crime. But even if he had said, he would have suffered. For if I say, he says, you will not believe. Furthermore, those who were not going to believe would have persevered in his death. And why would he not have suffered even more, if he had manifested himself as the god of another and thus as the adversary of the Creator? Therefore, it was not so that he might suffer that he then also showed himself to be another, but because they wanted to extort a confession from his mouth, and yet they would not have believed even if he had confessed, who ought to have recognized him from his works fulfilling the scriptures. Thus, it was his to hide himself, to whom recognition was owed even spontaneously. And yet, still stretching out his hand to them: from now on, he says, the Son of Man will be sitting at the right hand of the power of God. For he was suggesting that he is the one from Daniel's prophecy, the Son of Man, and from David's psalm, sitting at the right hand of God. And so, from this saying and the comparison of scripture, they were enlightened, whom he wanted to be understood: therefore, they say, you are the Son of God? Of which God, unless the one they alone knew? Of which God, unless the one they remembered saying to his Son in the psalm: sit at my right hand? But he responded: you say, as if: not I. However, he confirmed that he is what they said, while they were asking again. Whence, however, will you prove that he spoke interrogatively and not also confirmatively? Therefore, you are the Son of God, so that, because he had shown himself obliquely through the scriptures to be understood as the Son of God, they thus perceived: 'therefore, you are the Son of God,' which you do not want to say openly? And so, he also responded confirmatively, 'you say,' and thus his pronouncement was, so that they persevered in what his pronouncement implied.

pass_b_english: When Jesus says, 'Woe to the one who betrays the Son of Man,' the phrase 'woe' is clearly an expression of anger and offense, not just an empty threat. Unless, of course, the person who's about to commit this heinous crime is somehow innocent - but if that's the case, then the warning is meaningless. On the other hand, if the person is guilty, they'll definitely face punishment. Take the case of someone who knowingly lets one of their own followers commit a terrible crime - if that's what happened here, then don't try to justify the Creator's actions in the story of Adam by saying that your own god would have done the same thing. After all, if your god is all-powerful and all-knowing, then he's either ignorant, unable to prevent sin, or simply unwilling to intervene - and that would make him guilty of malicious neglect. I'm telling you, it's more reasonable to see the Creator as the one who's truly in charge here, rather than trying to elevate some other deity to the same level. Even Peter, who sometimes spoke out of turn, showed that he believed in a zealous god who wouldn't tolerate disobedience. And think about it - if Jesus was destined to be betrayed, it's only fitting that it happened with a kiss, given that he was the prophetic Christ, the Son of God who was loved by the people. When Jesus was brought before the council, they asked him point-blank if he was the Christ - and it's clear that they were asking about the Christ they knew from their own scriptures (Daniel 7:13). So why didn't Jesus reveal himself to them as the Christ of a different god, one who was opposed to the Creator? You might say it was so that he could suffer, but that doesn't add up - even if he had claimed to be the Christ, they still wouldn't have believed him, as he himself said (Luke 22:69). And if he had revealed himself as the Christ of a rival god, wouldn't that have just sealed his fate even more? No, the reason Jesus didn't reveal himself was that the council members were trying to trap him into making a confession, even though they wouldn't have believed him even if he had admitted it - after all, they should have recognized him as the Christ based on his miracles and teachings, which fulfilled the scriptures. Instead, Jesus chose to hide his true nature, even as he reached out to them - and when he said, 'From now on, the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God,' he was referencing the prophecies of Daniel and David (Psalm 110:1). The council members picked up on this and asked him if he was the Son of God - and it's obvious that they were thinking of the one God they knew, the God who had said to his Son, 'Sit at my right hand' (Psalm 110:1). Jesus responded by saying, 'You say so,' which might seem like a non-answer, but actually, he was confirming that he is indeed the Son of God. The question is, did he say this in a questioning tone, or was he making a statement? It seems to me that he was doing the latter, and that's why the council members persisted in their belief - they had finally understood that Jesus was claiming to be the Son of God, even if he didn't say it outright. Jesus had shown them through his teachings and scriptures that he was the Son of God, and they had put the pieces together - and that's why they reacted the way they did, because they knew that he was making a profound statement about his identity.

review.notes: Pass B is a paraphrase/interpretation rather than a translation, violating the requirement that it must not add to the sense. Specifically, Pass B adds significant interpretive commentary and narrative filler not present in the Latin, such as 'it's clear that they were asking about the Christ they knew from their own scriptures', 'it's obvious that they were thinking of the one God they knew', and 'they had finally understood that Jesus was claiming to be the Son of God, even if he didn't say it outright'. Furthermore, Pass B introduces specific scripture citations (Daniel 7:13, Luke 22:69, Psalm 110:1) that are not in the Locked Latin source; while the Latin alludes to these, the translator is required to match the actual words quoted or alluded to, and Pass B's inclusion of these as if they are the text's direct content (or adding them as external identifiers) deviates from the role of a translation of the provided text. Most importantly, Pass B adds 'Jesus' and 'the council members' as active agents in many places where the Latin is more abstract or uses different grammatical constructions, and adds 'it's more reasonable to see...' which is an interpretive expansion of 'suadeo igitur'.
reasons: Pass B is a paraphrase/interpretation that adds significant content not found in the source, such as 'it's clear that they were asking about the Christ they knew from their own scriptures' and 'they had finally understood that Jesus was claiming to be the Son of God, even if he didn't say it outright'. It also introduces specific verse citations (Daniel 7:13, Luke 22:69, Psalm 110:1) as part of the prose which are not in the Locked Latin.
